Anathoth
AN-uh-thoth
proper noun (place)
Hebrew Anathoth, a Levitical priestly town of Benjamin near Jerusalem; the home of the prophet Jeremiah and the place of Abiathar's banishment.

📖 Biblical Definition

Anathoth was a priestly town of Benjamin, a few miles northeast of Jerusalem, given to the Levites as a city of refuge and dwelling (Josh 21:18). It is bound up with two notable men. First, to Anathoth King Solomon banished the priest Abiathar, sparing his life for the ark's sake but thrusting him from the priesthood, and so fulfilling the LORD's word against the house of Eli (1 Kings 2:26-27). Second, and most famously, Anathoth was the birthplace and home of Jeremiah, "of the priests that were in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin" (Jer 1:1). The prophet met bitter hostility from his own townsmen, who plotted against his life and forbade him to prophesy (Jer 11:21-23); yet it was at Anathoth that God commanded him to buy the field of his cousin Hanameel, even as the Babylonians besieged the land, as a sign that "houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land" (Jer 32:6-15). Anathoth stands in the dictionary as the prophet's home that turned against him, and as the place of a purchased field of hope — a double witness that the servant of God is often rejected by his own, yet that the LORD's promises of restoration are sure even in the hour of judgment.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A priestly town of Benjamin near Jerusalem (Josh 21:18), the home of Jeremiah and the place of Abiathar's banishment; where Jeremiah's own townsmen plotted against him, yet where he bought a field of hope amid the siege (Jer 32).

ANATHOTH, proper noun. A Levitical priestly town of Benjamin near Jerusalem (Josh 21:18).

Where Solomon banished the priest Abiathar (1 Kings 2:26).

The birthplace and home of the prophet Jeremiah (Jer 1:1).

Where Jeremiah's own townsmen plotted against his life (Jer 11:21).

Where he bought the field of Hanameel as a sign of restoration (Jer 32:6-15).

📖 Key Scripture

Jer 1:1 — "The words of Jeremiah the son of Hilkiah, of the priests that were in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin:"

1 Kings 2:26 — "And unto Abiathar the priest said the king, Get thee to Anathoth, unto thine own fields; for thou art worthy of death: but I will not at this time put thee to death, because thou barest the ark of the Lord GOD before David my father, and because thou hast been afflicted in all wherein my father was afflicted."

Jer 11:21 — "Therefore thus saith the LORD of the men of Anathoth, that seek thy life, saying, Prophesy not in the name of the LORD, that thou die not by our hand:"

Jer 32:9 — "And I bought the field of Hanameel my uncle's son, that was in Anathoth, and weighed him the money, even seventeen shekels of silver."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Anathoth needs no defense from redefinition; its lessons are the rejection of the prophet by his own and the certainty of God's promises of restoration even under judgment.

expand to see more

Honor-at-home misreading. The world expects the prophet to be most honored where he is best known. Anathoth shows the opposite: Jeremiah's own townsmen, his kin and neighbors, sought his life and silenced his word, a foreshadowing of Him who came to His own and was not received (John 1:11). The dictionary holds the sober pattern: faithfulness to God's word often costs the servant the favor of his own people, and the messenger must not measure truth by the welcome it receives at home.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is hope grounded in God's promise. At the darkest hour, with the Babylonians at the walls, God told Jeremiah to buy a field at Anathoth as a pledge that the land would yet be redeemed. The dictionary commends the act of faith: the believer, even in the midst of judgment and loss, may stake his confidence on the sure word of God, who promises restoration beyond the ruin.
